questiontext.text: The V-model of software development is best described as a model that:

answer.text: Pairs each development (left) phase with a corresponding test (right) level, drawn in a V shape

feedback.text: Correct — the V-model lines up each development phase with the test level that later validates it.

answer.text: Repeats short build-test-release cycles with continuous customer feedback

feedback.text: That describes an Agile/iterative model, not the V-model.

answer.text: Delivers all testing in a single big-bang phase after every module is coded

feedback.text: The V-model deliberately spreads test design across the earlier phases; testing is not a single terminal phase.

answer.text: Builds a throwaway prototype first and derives requirements from it

feedback.text: That is prototyping; the V-model instead pairs planned phases with test levels.

generalfeedback.text: The V-model arranges the software life cycle as a V: development phases descend the left arm, test levels ascend the right arm, and each left phase is paired with the right-side level that validates it.

name.text: The left arm of the V

questiontext.text: In the V-model, the left (descending) arm represents:

answer.text: The development phases — requirements, then design, progressing down toward coding

feedback.text: Correct — the left arm descends through the development/definition phases.

answer.text: The test-execution levels, from unit up to acceptance

feedback.text: Those ascend the right arm, not the left.

answer.text: The maintenance and retirement activities after release

feedback.text: The V-model's arms cover development and testing, not the post-release phases.

answer.text: The project's budgeting and staffing plan

feedback.text: The arms model technical phases, not management planning.

generalfeedback.text: The left arm of the V descends through the successive development phases (requirements → system design → architectural design → detailed design), ending at coding at the vertex.

name.text: The right arm of the V

questiontext.text: In the V-model, the right (ascending) arm represents:

answer.text: The test levels — unit, then integration, system, and acceptance, progressing upward

feedback.text: Correct — the right arm ascends through the successive test-execution levels.

answer.text: The development phases from requirements down to coding

feedback.text: Those descend the left arm, not the right.

answer.text: The sequence of code reviews performed before any design begins

feedback.text: Reviews are static checks within phases; the right arm is the ladder of dynamic test levels.

answer.text: The rollback plan used if a release fails in production

feedback.text: That is an operations concern, not the right arm of the V.

generalfeedback.text: The right arm ascends through the test levels (unit → integration → system → acceptance). Each level validates the output of the development phase it is paired with on the left.

questiontext.text: At the bottom vertex of the V — the point joining the two arms — is:

feedback.text: Correct — coding sits at the vertex, joining the descending development arm to the ascending test arm.
Acceptance testing sits at the top of the right arm, paired with requirements, not at the vertex.
Requirements sits at the top of the left arm, not at the vertex.
System testing is a mid-upper level on the right arm, not the vertex.

generalfeedback.text: Coding is the lowest point of the V: it is where the left (development) arm turns into the right (testing) arm. From there testing climbs back up level by level.

questiontext.text: In the standard V-model, the requirements / user-requirements phase is paired with which test level?

feedback.text: Correct — acceptance testing validates the finished product against the user requirements.
Unit testing is paired with detailed/module design, not requirements.
Integration testing is paired with architectural design, not requirements.
System testing is paired with the system/high-level design, not the requirements phase.

generalfeedback.text: Standard V-model pairing: requirements ↔ acceptance testing. The requirements are the basis against which acceptance tests are designed and later executed.

name.text: System design pairs with which level

questiontext.text: In the standard V-model, the system (high-level / functional) design phase is paired with which test level?

feedback.text: Correct — system testing validates the integrated system against the system/functional design.
Acceptance testing is paired with the requirements phase, not the system design.
Integration testing is paired with architectural design, not system design.
Unit testing is paired with detailed/module design, not system design.

generalfeedback.text: Standard V-model pairing: system/high-level design ↔ system testing. The system design document is the basis for the system-level tests.

name.text: Architectural design pairs with which level

questiontext.text: In the standard V-model, the architectural / integration design phase is paired with which test level?

feedback.text: Correct — integration testing validates that the modules cooperate as the architecture prescribes.
Unit testing is paired with detailed/module design, not architectural design.
System testing is paired with the system/high-level design, not architectural design.
Acceptance testing is paired with the requirements phase, not architectural design.

generalfeedback.text: Standard V-model pairing: architectural/integration design ↔ integration testing. The architecture — which defines module interfaces and interactions — is the basis for the integration tests.

name.text: Detailed design pairs with which level

questiontext.text: In the standard V-model, the module / detailed design phase is paired with which test level?

feedback.text: Correct — unit testing validates each individual module against its detailed design.
Integration testing is paired with architectural design, not detailed design.
System testing is paired with the system/high-level design, not detailed design.
Acceptance testing is paired with the requirements phase, not detailed design.

generalfeedback.text: Standard V-model pairing: module/detailed design ↔ unit/component testing. The detailed design of each module is the basis for its unit tests. Detailed design leads directly into coding at the vertex.

questiontext.text: Reading the V-model the other way: acceptance testing is the test level paired with which development phase?

feedback.text: Correct — acceptance testing sits opposite requirements on the V.
That phase pairs with unit testing, not acceptance testing.
That phase pairs with integration testing, not acceptance testing.
Coding sits at the vertex; acceptance testing pairs with the requirements phase at the top of the left arm.

generalfeedback.text: Acceptance testing is the mirror image of the requirements phase: the user requirements written on the left are exactly what acceptance testing checks on the right.

questiontext.text: Reading the V-model the other way: unit / component testing is the test level paired with which development phase?

feedback.text: Correct — unit testing sits opposite detailed design on the V.
That phase pairs with acceptance testing, not unit testing.
That phase pairs with system testing, not unit testing.
That phase pairs with integration testing, not unit testing.

generalfeedback.text: Unit testing is the mirror image of detailed design: the internal behaviour designed for each module is exactly what its unit tests check.

questiontext.text: On the left arm of the V, activities are chiefly verification. Verification asks:

answer.text: "Are we building the product right?" — checking each phase's output conforms to its specification, via reviews and other static checks

feedback.text: Correct — verification is conformance-to-spec, largely through static techniques such as reviews and inspections.

answer.text: "Are we building the right product?" — checking the delivered software meets the users' actual needs

feedback.text: That is validation, which lives on the right arm.

answer.text: Only running the compiled program against live user data

feedback.text: Running the program is dynamic execution (validation-side activity); verification is largely static.

answer.text: Measuring the server's throughput under peak load

feedback.text: That is performance testing, not the meaning of verification.

generalfeedback.text: Verification (left arm) asks "did we build the product right?" — it confirms each artifact conforms to its specification, mainly through static checks (reviews, inspections, walkthroughs) and early test design.

questiontext.text: On the right arm of the V, activities are chiefly validation. Validation asks:

answer.text: "Are we building the right product?" — running the software to confirm it meets the users' actual needs

feedback.text: Correct — validation is dynamic execution that checks fitness for the users' real needs.

answer.text: "Are we building the product right?" — reviewing documents for conformance to their specification

feedback.text: That is verification, which lives on the left arm.

answer.text: Confirming the requirements document is internally consistent, without executing anything

feedback.text: That static review is a verification activity, not validation.

answer.text: Estimating the project schedule and cost

feedback.text: That is project management, not validation.

generalfeedback.text: Validation (right arm) asks "did we build the right product?" — it executes the software (dynamic testing) to confirm it satisfies the users' real needs. Acceptance/UAT is the clearest validation activity.

questiontext.text: A defining idea of the V-model is early test design. This means:

answer.text: The tests for each level are planned and designed during the paired left-side phase, even though they are executed later

feedback.text: Correct — e.g. acceptance tests are designed while requirements are written, long before execution.

answer.text: All tests are both designed and executed only after coding is finished

feedback.text: That is the very practice the V-model's early test design is meant to replace.

answer.text: Testers are hired only at the end of the project

feedback.text: Early test design means testers engage from the start, not the end.

answer.text: Coding is skipped and replaced by test scripts

feedback.text: Coding still happens at the vertex; test design merely starts early.

generalfeedback.text: Early test design: as each left-side phase produces its artifact, the tests for the matching right-side level are designed there and then (acceptance tests with requirements, system tests with system design, and so on). Execution still happens later, up the right arm.

questiontext.text: In the V-model, coding (implementation) sits at the bottom vertex, joining the descending development arm to the ascending test arm.

feedback.text: Correct — coding is the lowest point of the V, where development turns into testing.
Coding does sit at the vertex; the two arms meet at implementation.

generalfeedback.text: The V descends through the development phases to coding at the vertex, then ascends through the test levels. Coding is the turning point that joins the two arms.

name.text: Testing is not only at the very end

questiontext.text: In the V-model, all testing work begins only after coding is complete, with nothing test-related happening during the earlier development phases.

feedback.text: This is the misconception the V-model corrects: test design starts early, during the paired left-side phases.
Correct — although test execution happens later, test design/planning for each level begins during its paired development phase.

generalfeedback.text: The whole point of the V-model over a naive waterfall is that testing is not deferred to the end: the tests for each level are designed alongside the matching development phase, even though they are executed up the right arm afterwards.

questiontext.text: In the V-model, which document is the test basis (the source the test cases are derived from) for acceptance testing?

feedback.text: Correct — acceptance tests are derived from the requirements, its paired left-side artifact.
That is the basis for unit testing, not acceptance testing.
That is the basis for integration testing, not acceptance testing.

answer.text: The source code of individual functions

feedback.text: Acceptance testing is derived from user requirements, not from reading the code.

generalfeedback.text: Each right-side level draws its test basis from its paired left-side artifact. Acceptance testing ↔ requirements, so the requirements specification is the basis for the acceptance tests.

questiontext.text: In the V-model, which document is the test basis for system testing?

feedback.text: Correct — system tests are derived from the system/functional design, its paired left-side artifact.
That is the basis for acceptance testing, not system testing.

answer.text: The detailed design of a single module

feedback.text: That is the basis for unit testing, not system testing.
That is the basis for integration testing, not system testing.

generalfeedback.text: System testing ↔ system/high-level design. The system design specification defines the whole system's functional behaviour, and system testing checks the integrated system against it.

questiontext.text: In the V-model, which document is the test basis for integration testing?

feedback.text: Correct — the architecture defines how modules interface, and integration tests are derived from it.
That is the basis for acceptance testing, not integration testing.
That is the basis for system testing, not integration testing.

answer.text: The detailed design of a single module

feedback.text: That is the basis for unit testing, not integration testing.

generalfeedback.text: Integration testing ↔ architectural design. Because the architecture specifies module interfaces and interactions, it is exactly the basis against which integration tests are designed.

questiontext.text: In the V-model, which document is the test basis for unit / component testing?

feedback.text: Correct — the detailed design defines each module's internal behaviour, and unit tests are derived from it.
That is the basis for integration testing, not unit testing.
That is the basis for system testing, not unit testing.
That is the basis for acceptance testing, not unit testing.

generalfeedback.text: Unit testing ↔ detailed/module design. The detailed design describes what each individual module should do internally, so it is the basis for that module's unit tests.

questiontext.text: Your team has just finished the architectural design, which specifies how the modules interface and interact. Which test level (per the V-model) is designed to validate this phase's output?

feedback.text: Correct — architectural design ↔ integration testing; integration tests check that the modules cooperate as the architecture prescribes.
Unit testing validates detailed design (single-module behaviour), not the architecture's inter-module interfaces.
Acceptance testing validates the requirements, not the architectural design.
System testing validates the system/high-level design, not the architectural/interface design.

generalfeedback.text: Match the phase to its paired level: architectural design ↔ integration testing. Because the architecture defines module interfaces, integration testing is what checks those interfaces work once modules are combined.

questiontext.text: Your team has just finished the detailed (module) design, which specifies each module's internal behaviour. Which test level (per the V-model) is designed to validate this phase's output?

feedback.text: Correct — detailed design ↔ unit testing; unit tests check each module against its detailed design.
Integration testing validates the architectural design (inter-module interfaces), not a single module's internal behaviour.
System testing validates the system/high-level design, not the detailed design of one module.
Acceptance testing validates the requirements, not the detailed design.

generalfeedback.text: Match the phase to its paired level: detailed/module design ↔ unit testing. The detailed design of each module is what its unit tests check.

questiontext.text: A team holds an inspection meeting to review the requirements specification for completeness and consistency, without running any code. In V-model terms this activity is:

feedback.text: Correct — reviewing an artifact for conformance, with no execution, is verification.
Validation involves executing the software; a document review does not.
Acceptance testing executes the finished product with users; a requirements inspection is a static review.
Integration testing dynamically exercises combined modules; a requirements review runs nothing.

generalfeedback.text: Left arm = verification (static: reviews, inspections, "building the product right"). A requirements inspection runs no code, so it is a verification activity, not a validation (dynamic) one.

questiontext.text: Users run the finished software against their real business scenarios to confirm it meets their needs. In V-model terms this activity is:

feedback.text: Correct — executing the software to confirm fitness for user needs is validation.
Verification is static conformance checking; executing the product against user needs is validation.

answer.text: A design review of the architecture

feedback.text: That is a static left-arm activity; running the software with users is dynamic validation.
Unit testing exercises single modules; this scenario is whole-product acceptance, a validation activity.

generalfeedback.text: Right arm = validation (dynamic: executing the software, "building the right product"). Running the finished software against real user needs is the archetypal validation activity — acceptance/UAT.

questiontext.text: Why does the V-model have the tests for each level designed during the paired left-side phase rather than after coding?

answer.text: Designing tests against each artifact exposes ambiguities/defects in that artifact early, and leaves the tests ready to execute when the code arrives

feedback.text: Correct — early test design finds specification/design faults sooner and prepares tests in advance.

answer.text: It lets the team skip writing the requirements and design documents

feedback.text: Early test design depends on those documents as its basis; it does not eliminate them.

answer.text: It removes the need to ever execute the tests

feedback.text: Tests are still executed later up the right arm; only their design is moved earlier.

answer.text: It converts the sequential model into an iterative, Agile one

feedback.text: The V-model remains sequential; early test design does not make it iterative.

generalfeedback.text: Designing tests while each artifact is fresh forces careful reading of that artifact, so ambiguities and defects surface early (cheap to fix), and the tests are ready to run the moment the corresponding code exists.

questiontext.text: According to the V-model, what testing activity should occur during the requirements phase (before any code exists)?

answer.text: Designing and planning the acceptance tests (the level paired with requirements)

feedback.text: Correct — acceptance tests are designed while requirements are written; they execute later.

answer.text: Executing the acceptance tests against the delivered system

feedback.text: Execution comes later, up the right arm; during requirements the acceptance tests are only designed.

answer.text: Designing the unit tests for each module

feedback.text: Unit tests are designed later, during detailed design — the phase paired with unit testing.

answer.text: No testing activity of any kind can happen yet

feedback.text: The V-model's early test design means acceptance-test design begins right here, at the requirements phase.

generalfeedback.text: Requirements ↔ acceptance testing, so the requirements phase is exactly when acceptance tests are designed. That design work (though executed much later) is part of the phase's early test design.

name.text: Why unit pairs with detailed design

questiontext.text: Why does the V-model pair unit testing specifically with the detailed (module) design phase?

answer.text: The detailed design specifies each module's internal behaviour, which is exactly what unit tests check

feedback.text: Correct — the artifact that defines a module's internals is the natural basis for its unit tests.

answer.text: The detailed design lists the users' business goals, which unit tests confirm

feedback.text: Business goals live in the requirements (paired with acceptance testing), not the detailed design.

answer.text: The detailed design fixes the interfaces between modules, which unit tests exercise

feedback.text: Inter-module interfaces belong to the architecture (paired with integration testing); unit tests target one module.

answer.text: Because unit tests can only be written after the whole system is designed

feedback.text: Unit tests are designed at the detailed-design phase, not after all higher-level design is finished.

generalfeedback.text: Each pairing matches a test level to the artifact that is its natural basis. The detailed design describes a single module's internal behaviour, so it is precisely what unit/component testing verifies.

questiontext.text: Why does the V-model pair integration testing specifically with the architectural design phase?

answer.text: The architecture defines the module interfaces and interactions, which is exactly what integration testing exercises

feedback.text: Correct — the artifact that specifies how modules connect is the natural basis for integration tests.

answer.text: The architecture describes each module's internal algorithm, which integration tests check

feedback.text: Internal algorithms are detailed design (paired with unit testing); integration testing targets interactions.

answer.text: The architecture states the user acceptance criteria, which integration tests confirm

feedback.text: Acceptance criteria come from the requirements (paired with acceptance testing), not the architecture.

answer.text: Because integration tests can only run once the full system is deployed to users

feedback.text: Integration testing runs after unit testing and before system/acceptance testing, not only at deployment.

generalfeedback.text: The architectural design specifies how modules are decomposed and how they talk to one another, so it is the natural basis for integration testing, which checks that combined modules interact correctly.

questiontext.text: In the V-model, dynamic test execution (actually running the software) is concentrated on which side, and under which term?

feedback.text: Correct — the right arm's ascending test levels execute the software; this is validation.
The left arm is mostly static (reviews, test design) — verification — not dynamic execution.
The left arm is verification, and it is largely static rather than dynamic execution.
The right arm is validation, not verification; verification is the left-arm term.

generalfeedback.text: Left arm = verification (mostly static: reviews plus early test design). Right arm = validation (dynamic execution of the built software, level by level). Dynamic test execution therefore lives on the right arm, as validation.

name.text: Acceptance tests can be written from requirements

questiontext.text: In the V-model, the acceptance test cases can be designed as soon as the requirements are agreed — that is, before any code is written.

feedback.text: Correct — requirements ↔ acceptance testing, so acceptance tests are designed during the requirements phase (executed much later).
Because acceptance testing is paired with requirements, its tests can indeed be designed once requirements are agreed, well before coding.

generalfeedback.text: Early test design applies most visibly at the top of the V: the requirements are the basis for acceptance testing, so acceptance test cases can be authored as soon as requirements are settled — long before the code exists.

questiontext.text: While writing the architectural design document, a team simultaneously drafts the integration test cases for the interfaces it defines. This practice illustrates:

answer.text: Early test design — designing a level's tests during its paired left-side phase (architecture ↔ integration testing)

feedback.text: Correct — the integration tests are designed during the architectural phase they are paired with.

answer.text: A mistake — integration tests must only be written after coding is complete

feedback.text: The V-model deliberately encourages designing these tests early, during architectural design.

answer.text: Acceptance testing, because interfaces face the user

feedback.text: Interfaces between modules pair with integration testing; acceptance testing pairs with requirements.

answer.text: An Agile sprint, because design and testing overlap

feedback.text: Overlapping test design with a phase is core V-model practice, not specifically Agile.

generalfeedback.text: This is exactly the V-model's early test design: each left-side phase produces both its development artifact and the design of the tests for its paired right-side level. Architecture ↔ integration testing.

name.text: Where an interface mismatch is caught

questiontext.text: Two subsystems exchange data in incompatible formats — a fault in how they interface. In the V-model, at which test level is this fault first targeted, and during which phase were those tests designed?

answer.text: Caught at integration testing; those tests were designed during architectural design

feedback.text: Correct — inter-module interface faults are the target of integration testing, whose basis is the architecture.

answer.text: Caught at unit testing; those tests were designed during detailed design

feedback.text: Unit testing exercises a single module in isolation; a cross-subsystem interface mismatch is an integration concern.

answer.text: Caught at acceptance testing; those tests were designed during the requirements phase

feedback.text: Acceptance testing checks user needs on the whole product; an interface-format mismatch is targeted earlier, at integration.

answer.text: Caught at system testing; those tests were designed during detailed design

feedback.text: The level is wrong (interfaces ↔ integration) and system tests are designed during system design, not detailed design.

generalfeedback.text: Interface/interaction faults between modules are exactly what integration testing targets, and integration testing is paired with — and designed during — the architectural design phase.

name.text: A product that misses user needs

questiontext.text: A delivered system conforms perfectly to its design documents, yet fails to meet what users actually needed. In the V-model, which level is meant to expose this, and is it verification or validation?

answer.text: Acceptance testing — a validation activity, checking the product against real user needs

feedback.text: Correct — "right product?" is validation, and acceptance testing (paired with requirements) is where user-need gaps surface.

answer.text: Unit testing — a verification activity, checking each module against its detailed design

feedback.text: Conformance to a module's design is verification; it cannot reveal that the whole product misses user needs.

answer.text: Integration testing — a validation activity, checking module interfaces

feedback.text: Integration testing targets interfaces (and is dynamic validation of that scope), not overall fitness for user needs.

answer.text: A design review — a validation activity, checking the requirements document

feedback.text: A document review is static verification, not validation, and it cannot confirm real-world fitness.

generalfeedback.text: "Built the product right" (matches design) is verification; "built the right product" (meets user needs) is validation. A system can pass all verification yet fail validation — acceptance testing, paired with requirements, is where that gap shows.

name.text: How the V improves on waterfall

questiontext.text: Compared with the classic waterfall model, the V-model's chief improvement for testing is that it:

answer.text: Involves testing early — the tests for each level are designed in parallel with the matching development phase, instead of only after coding

feedback.text: Correct — the V-model makes test design a first-class activity of every development phase.

answer.text: Removes the design and requirements phases entirely

feedback.text: The V-model keeps all those phases; it adds a paired test level to each.

answer.text: Lets requirements change freely at any point without cost

feedback.text: The V-model is still sequential; late requirement changes remain costly.
That is prototyping/Agile; the V-model is still document-driven.

generalfeedback.text: Waterfall pushes testing to the end. The V-model pairs every development phase with a test level and designs those tests early, so defects in requirements and design are found sooner — its main testing advantage over waterfall.

questiontext.text: Even with its early test design, the V-model still inherits which key weakness of the waterfall model?

answer.text: It is sequential and rigid — phases run in order, so it adapts poorly to changing requirements

feedback.text: Correct — early test design does not remove the underlying sequential, plan-driven structure.

answer.text: It never tests the software at all

feedback.text: The V-model tests thoroughly, level by level; that is not the shared weakness.

answer.text: It has no defined requirements phase

feedback.text: Requirements is the top-left phase of the V; it is clearly defined.
The V-model is heavily document-driven, the opposite of forbidding design docs.

generalfeedback.text: The V-model reorganises when tests are designed, but it keeps waterfall's linear, phase-by-phase flow. It therefore struggles when requirements change late — the same rigidity waterfall is criticised for.

questiontext.text: Compared with Agile/iterative development, the V-model is a poor fit when:

answer.text: Requirements are volatile and stakeholders need early, working increments to react to

feedback.text: Correct — the V-model assumes stable, well-understood requirements up front and produces no early prototypes.

answer.text: Requirements are stable and well understood before design begins

feedback.text: That is precisely where the V-model works well, not poorly.

answer.text: A clear phase structure with a matching test level for each phase is desired

feedback.text: That is a strength of the V-model, not a poor-fit situation.

answer.text: Formal documentation and traceability are required by the domain

feedback.text: The V-model's document-driven rigor suits such domains; it is not a poor fit there.

generalfeedback.text: Agile delivers working increments iteratively and welcomes change; the V-model plans all phases up front with no early prototypes. When requirements are volatile and early feedback is essential, the V-model fits poorly and Agile is preferred.

questiontext.text: Claim: "The V-model shows that every testing activity — including test design — happens strictly after coding, so testers need not be involved during requirements or design." Is this claim correct?

feedback.text: This is a common misconception. In the V-model, each level's tests are designed during its paired left-side phase, so testers engage from the start.
Correct — although test execution ascends the right arm after coding, the design of each level's tests occurs during its paired development phase.

generalfeedback.text: The trap: confusing test execution (which does come after coding) with test design (which the V-model deliberately moves early). Acceptance tests are designed with requirements, system tests with system design, and so on — so the claim is false.

questiontext.text: Reading the V from the coding vertex outward, which test level sits furthest from the vertex (paired with the topmost left-side phase)?

answer.text: Acceptance testing (paired with requirements, at the top of the V)

feedback.text: Correct — requirements is the topmost left phase, so its partner, acceptance testing, is the outermost right level.
Unit testing is nearest the vertex, not furthest — detailed design is the lowest left phase.
Integration testing is a middle level, not the outermost.
System testing is upper-middle, but acceptance testing (with requirements) sits above it.

generalfeedback.text: The higher a phase sits on the left arm, the higher its paired level sits on the right. Requirements is the top-left phase, so acceptance testing is the outermost (furthest-from-vertex) right-side level.

questiontext.text: Which test level sits closest to the coding vertex (paired with the lowest left-side design phase)?

answer.text: Unit / component testing (paired with detailed design)

feedback.text: Correct — detailed design is the lowest left phase, leading into coding, so its partner unit testing is nearest the vertex.
Acceptance testing is furthest from the vertex, not closest.
System testing is upper-middle, not closest to the vertex.
Integration testing is closer than system/acceptance, but unit testing is nearer the vertex.

generalfeedback.text: Detailed design is the lowest left phase (it flows straight into coding at the vertex), so its paired level, unit testing, is the first level up the right arm and the closest to the vertex.

name.text: Order of test execution up the right arm

questiontext.text: Ascending the right arm from the vertex, in what order are the test levels executed?

feedback.text: Correct — testing climbs from the smallest scope (unit) to the whole product against user needs (acceptance).
That is the reverse; execution ascends from unit upward, not downward.
Unit precedes integration, and system precedes acceptance; this ordering is scrambled.
Unit is first, not third; system testing comes after integration.

generalfeedback.text: Up the right arm the scope widens: individual modules (unit), then their combinations (integration), then the whole system (system), then the product against user needs (acceptance). Execution order is unit → integration → system → acceptance.

questiontext.text: The pair of guiding questions "Are we building the product right?" and "Are we building the right product?" map to the two arms of the V. Which arm/term answers "Are we building the right product?"

feedback.text: Correct — "right product?" (fitness for user needs) is validation, done dynamically up the right arm.
Verification answers "building the product right?" (conformance to spec), not "the right product?".
The left arm is verification, not validation.
The right arm is validation; verification is the left-arm term.

generalfeedback.text: "Building the product right?" = verification (left, static conformance). "Building the right product?" = validation (right, dynamic fitness for user needs). The second question is answered by the right arm's validation.

questiontext.text: Fill both blanks consistently with the standard V-model: the requirements specification is the test basis for ______, and the detailed design is the test basis for ______.

feedback.text: Correct — requirements ↔ acceptance testing, detailed design ↔ unit testing.
Requirements pair with acceptance (not system) and detailed design pairs with unit (not integration).
The pairings are reversed — requirements go with acceptance, detailed design with unit.
The first is right, but detailed design pairs with unit testing, not integration testing.

generalfeedback.text: Standard pairings: requirements ↔ acceptance, system design ↔ system, architecture ↔ integration, detailed design ↔ unit. So requirements → acceptance testing and detailed design → unit testing.

name.text: Meaning of a matching validation per phase

questiontext.text: An advantage often cited for the V-model is that "each development phase has a matching test level." What does this actually buy the project?

answer.text: Every left-side artifact has a designated right-side level that will validate it, so no phase's output is left unchecked and traceability from tests to artifacts is clear

feedback.text: Correct — the explicit pairing gives every artifact a home for its verification/validation and clear test-to-artifact traceability.

answer.text: It guarantees the software will contain no defects after acceptance testing

feedback.text: No model guarantees zero defects; the pairing improves coverage and traceability, not perfection.

answer.text: It lets the team run all test levels simultaneously with the design phases

feedback.text: Tests are designed early but executed sequentially up the right arm, not all at once.

answer.text: It eliminates the need for requirements traceability

feedback.text: The pairing strengthens traceability; it does not remove the need for it.

generalfeedback.text: Pairing each phase with a test level means every artifact produced on the left has an explicit level responsible for checking it, giving structured coverage and clear traceability between tests and the artifacts they exercise.

name.text: When system tests are ideally designed

questiontext.text: Applying early test design consistently, at which point are the system test cases ideally designed (even though they run later)?

answer.text: During the system / high-level design phase (its paired left-side phase)

feedback.text: Correct — system testing ↔ system design, so system tests are designed during system design.
The requirements phase is when acceptance tests are designed; system tests pair with system design.

answer.text: Only after acceptance testing has finished

feedback.text: System testing precedes acceptance testing; its tests are designed far earlier, at system design.
Detailed design is when unit tests are designed; system tests pair with system/high-level design.

generalfeedback.text: Early test design places each level's test design in its paired phase. System testing ↔ system/high-level design, so the system tests are ideally designed during the system design phase, then executed up the right arm after integration.

name.text: Cost of a late requirements change

questiontext.text: Late in a V-model project, a user requirement changes. Why is this typically expensive to accommodate?

answer.text: Because the model is sequential, the change ripples through the already-completed design, code, and every paired test level's artifacts, all of which must be revised

feedback.text: Correct — a requirements change invalidates downstream artifacts and their paired (e.g. acceptance) tests, and there is no iterative mechanism to absorb it cheaply.

answer.text: Because the V-model has no requirements phase, so the change has nowhere to be recorded

feedback.text: Requirements is the top-left phase of the V; the problem is rework downstream, not a missing phase.

answer.text: Because test design cannot begin until the change is coded

feedback.text: The V-model designs tests early; the cost comes from reworking completed sequential artifacts, not from delayed test design.

answer.text: Because acceptance testing is unrelated to the requirements and must be redone from scratch regardless

feedback.text: Acceptance testing is tightly paired with requirements; that pairing is precisely why the change forces acceptance-test rework.

generalfeedback.text: The V-model's rigidity means a late requirements change forces revisiting the system/architecture/detailed designs, the code, and each paired test level (acceptance tests most directly). Unlike an iterative model, it cannot absorb such change in a later increment, so late changes are costly.
